1:
That Miriam led the revolt is agreed, and Ellicott gives the grammatical proof: her name stands first, the verb rendered spake is feminine, and the judgment afterwards fell on her and not on Aaron, who seems to have yielded to her as he had earlier yielded to the people over the golden calf. Gill puts it in terms of outcome, that she was first in the transgression and so alone punished, while Aaron was drawn in, confessed and was forgiven. Wesley adds that as first mover she was the more eminently punished. Henry dwells on who these people were: not merely eminent in religion, a prophetess and a high priest once joint commissioners for the deliverance of Israel, but Moses' own brother and sister, so that the quarrel was of the hardest kind to bear. Calvin turns the fact into an argument. Had Aaron and Miriam always supported their brother, however holy that harmony was, it would have been alleged against them as a deceitful conspiracy; that his own family contended for the supremacy removed all suspicion of family favour and showed that Moses was upheld by the power of God alone.

Who the Ethiopian woman was, and whether she was the real grievance, divides them. Ellicott sets out the case for Zipporah, since Cushites included an Asiatic division and a prophet couples Cushan with Midian, and then rejects it: the words point to a recent occurrence rather than one more than forty years old, and the murmuring is tied expressly to the woman herself and not to any influence her relations had gained. He concludes Zipporah was probably dead. Wesley keeps both options open, noting that Cush generally means Arabia rather than Ethiopia proper, and that if Zipporah is meant the quarrel was not the marriage but Moses being swayed by her family in choosing the seventy elders. Henry guesses at a private falling out between Zipporah and Miriam, one peevish reflection drawing on another. Keil states the claim at face value before it is judged, the high priest who bears the congregation's rights in the Urim and Thummim and the prophetess asking whether they too are not organs of divine revelation, and he notes that the remark that the Lord heard is set down to prepare for his judicial interposition. Clarke cuts through by separating the ostensible cause from the real, which was jealousy of Moses' power, and observes that although this government carried no gain and no honour but what came from God, the love of power is natural to men, who will sacrifice honour, pleasure and profit to it.

The verse praising Moses' meekness raises two questions at once, whether he could have written it and what it means. Ellicott reports its use as an argument against Mosaic authorship and answers that the inference is unfounded either way: the writer of the closing chapter of Deuteronomy may have inserted it, but such an objective statement is perfectly consistent with true humility, least of all objectionable in men like Moses and Paul, ready to sacrifice their own personality to their cause. Gill and Wesley both allow a later hand, Gill suggesting Joshua or Ezra under the same inspiration and Wesley some succeeding prophet; Wesley adds the difficulty that we often read of Moses in anger, concluding only that the law made nothing perfect. Clarke attacks the translation instead. The word comes from a root meaning to depress or afflict, so the sense is that Moses was more afflicted than any man of that land, borne down by governing an ungrateful people; the very power they envied was oppressive to its possessor. Calvin reads the parenthesis as explaining why God acted unprompted, since the meek man imposed patience on himself and made no complaint, and draws from it that the silence of long-suffering is more effectual before God than any cries.
4:
The suddenness of the summons is read as significant by everyone who mentions it. Gill gives two reasons: God acted as one greatly provoked, and before the complaint could spread among a people already disposed to mutiny; the speed also proved Moses had not solicited it, no time being allowed him to apply. Clarke says the same more briefly, that the suddenness shows at once the importance of the case and the displeasure. Wesley reads the command to come out as a summons from their private dwellings to learn God's pleasure and their own doom, and finds a further mark of displeasure in their being kept at the door rather than admitted as Aaron used to be. Ellicott is careful that nothing implies Miriam entered the tabernacle itself; the three were called out of the camp to the entrance of the court, there being only one court then. Calvin sees the place doing part of the work, its sanctity casting down a haughtiness grown out of forgetfulness of God, their separation from Moses forcing them to confess an inferiority they had denied. Henry sets it out as a trial at law, the judges of old sitting in the gate and the accused called to the bar, and draws the moral that the more silent we are in our own cause the more God is engaged to plead it, since an innocent man need say little when the judge himself will be his advocate.

On the two ordinary modes of revelation Calvin is most exact about the words. The term used is not the one meaning a prophecy but the one expressing a visible appearance, ratifying the truth of God's word to the eyes and all the senses; such sights were frequent to the patriarchs before the Law, and a prophet promising a fullness of revelation under Christ names the same pair. The point of naming them, Calvin says, is to withdraw Moses from the common condition by a special privilege, so Aaron and Miriam should see how far behind they stood. Wesley states the conclusion bluntly: if they are prophets, still there is a difference among prophets, and God does not put equal honour on all. Clarke supplies a reason why Moses could not be dealt with in enigmas: he was to receive laws whose precepts must be within reach of the meanest capacity. Ellicott works on the rendering, preferring if there be among you a prophet of Jehovah, and noting that the Greek and Latin versions attach the divine name to the earlier clause.

Mouth to mouth is glossed by each in his own way. Gill takes it as free and familiar speech, as one friend to another, without the consternation that sometimes overtook the prophets, and reports Aben Ezra's sense that it means without a mediator, not by an angel. Wesley makes it distinct and articulate, not by an interpreter nor by shadows in the fancy, and contrasts the dark speeches given to others, the boiling pot shown to Jeremiah and the chariot to Ezekiel. On the similitude he denies that Moses saw the essence of God, which no man can see and live, proposing instead a singular manifestation of glory, and adds that the Son appeared to him in a human shape taken up for the time as a foretaste of the incarnation. Ellicott handles the word philologically, noting it is the term of the second commandment and stands beside its companion in a verse of Job. Clarke observes that the word for faithful means a prefect or superintendent, a title given to ambassadors. Calvin notes how the apostle uses the clause to prove Moses inferior to Christ, a servant in the house against its builder. Wesley closes on the departure, that the removal of God's presence is the saddest token of displeasure, and that he never departs till we drive him away.
10:
Ellicott notices that the cloud's going is described by a different word from the one used when it is taken up for a march: the lifting was the signal to break camp, this was the token of a presence withdrawn. Gill and Wesley both restrict the movement, Gill saying it rose higher or removed some distance from the most holy place where it used to rest, Wesley that it left not the whole tabernacle but the part it had come to. Henry needs only a sentence for the sequence: when God goes, evil comes. On the leprosy itself Ellicott and Wesley agree on the point that matters, that a whiteness covering the whole body would ordinarily have meant the man was clean, but that this rule did not hold where the stroke came immediately from God, as with Moses' hand and with Gehazi; Wesley calls this kind the most virulent and incurable, precisely because the whiteness was sudden rather than reached by degrees. Henry takes the disfigurement as fitted to the offence, quoting a bishop's remark that a foul tongue was justly punished with a foul face, and adding the contrast that Moses needed a veil to hide his glory while Miriam needed one to hide her shame.

That Aaron went unpunished is treated as requiring explanation rather than as an oversight. Henry offers two reasons: God would put a difference between those who mislead and those who are misled, and Aaron's office, though it did not save him from displeasure, secured him from this particular token of it, which would have suspended him from serving at a time when there were only three priests in Israel and left a lasting blot on his family. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by the harder road, that had Aaron been smitten his sacred character must have suffered and the priesthood itself fallen into contempt; and he turns it at once on his own readers, observing how many priests and preachers who deserved exposure have been spared for the sake of the character they bore, so that the ministry might not be blamed, while the just God visits their transgressions some other way. Nothing, he adds, discredits the work of God so much as the miscarriages of those who minister in holy things. Wesley gives the plainer version, that God would not have his worship interrupted or dishonoured. Gill and Clarke both return to Miriam's being first in the transgression as the sufficient ground.

Aaron's plea is read closely. Ellicott notes that the word rendered alas is an exclamation of entreaty rather than of lamentation, used toward superiors, and that the request is not that the guilt be shifted elsewhere but that they be spared the punishment their sin deserved. Gill reports the Jewish reading upon me, my lord, be all the blame, and marks the reversal in Aaron calling a younger brother his lord. Calvin makes that reversal the point: the dread of punishment was the best medicine for his disease of ambition, and in confessing folly he does not do what most people do and hide a transgression under the plea of thoughtlessness. On the comparison with a dead child, Ellicott reports that the scribes are said to have altered this text, and gives the severer original, adding that the leper was as one dead both in being shut out and in defiling by touch as a corpse does; Wesley makes it a still-born child putrefied in the womb. Keil defends the unusual construction of the plea against those who would emend it. Calvin closes on Moses, taking his immediate intercession as proof of the meekness just claimed for him, so that Miriam's only hope now lay in the dignity she had refused to allow him.
14:
The comparison God draws is domestic, and the commentators take its force from the custom behind it. Ellicott records that spitting in a person's presence, still more in the face, counts in the East as the extreme sign of abhorrence and indignation, and offers the alternative rendering in her presence. Clarke adds that a father did this only under great provocation and strong irritation, and that when it happened the child was banished from his presence for seven days; from which he draws the argument the verse implies, that if such severity was allowed between child and parent it can hardly be excessive where a creature has rebelled against the Creator. He presses the sentence for what it cost, since to be shut out of the camp was to be debarred from the presence of God, who is represented as dwelling among the people, and to a soul that knows the blessedness of communion with him seven days of such darkness would be intolerable. Wesley takes the shame to mean withdrawing oneself, as Jonathan withdrew from his father's table; Keil reads it as keeping herself hidden out of pure shame.

Why seven days and not another number is answered from the leprosy law. Ellicott points out that seven was both the period a suspected leper was shut up in the first instance and the period a cleansed leper tarried outside his tent before the sacrifices were offered for him, and then states the reversal plainly: the woman who had put herself on a level with the divinely appointed head of the nation was to be excluded for seven days from privileges the humblest member of the congregation enjoyed. Keil makes the same proportion explicit, that in exaggerating the worth of her own prophetic gift she had exalted herself above the congregation, and was therefore struck with the one disease that puts a person outside the number of the people of God; he also notes that the sentence carried its own limit, restoration being promised after the seven days were endured. Gill sharpens the point by separating cure from punishment: Miriam was no doubt healed at once, and the exclusion that followed was penalty and not treatment.

That the whole nation waited for her is read by Wesley as a mark of respect rather than of delay, and he gives two reasons for God so ordering it, that she should not be overwhelmed by so public a rebuke, and that the gift of prophecy should not fall into contempt through her. Gill explains the mechanics of the resumption, the cloud having returned to the tabernacle and been taken up again as the signal for motion, and he places the next camp eight miles from Hazeroth on one authority, dating the arrival to the end of Sivan. Ellicott and Keil both identify the encampment in Paran with Kadesh, Keil locating it near a spring on the heights south of Beersheba. Gill and Clarke then look forward from the same spot to what happened there. Israel was now very near the promised land and might quickly have entered it, but for the affair of the spies which kept them out thirty-eight years longer; and Clarke turns that into the lesson he wants, that a journey of a few weeks took thirty-eight years, and that much ground may be lost in the divine life by a single act of unfaithfulness.
